pairs.question: Explain Git.
pairs.left:
Git is a tool that keeps selected versions of a project so you can inspect an earlier version or restore its file contents later. It records a snapshot of the project each time you deliberately make a record called a commit. Saving a file in your editor does not make a commit, and Git does not automatically record every edit.

Imagine you are making a digital painting. You finish the outline, prepare that version for Git to record, and make a commit. Later, you add a blue sky and prepare and commit that version too. The blue sky commit keeps the earlier outline in the project's history.
pairs.right: Git tracks your painting so every change was recorded as you worked, including ordinary editor saves. You can later recover any brushstroke because the history is complete.

pairs.question: What do Git branches add? Keep the digital painting example.
pairs.audience: I understand saving a file and making a commit.
pairs.left: Git branches let you keep developing the painting in two directions, such as a daytime scene and a night scene. Earlier commits already remain in history, so what branches add is a way to continue each direction separately. Create a branch named night at the current commit, then switch to night before you darken the sky and commit.
pairs.right: After you commit the night sky, a new commit on that branch would overwrite an earlier committed version of the daytime painting. Branches are needed to keep the earlier version.
